title: Holy Food and Unblemished Offerings
summary: Priests must treat the sacred offerings with care: a priest who is unclean may not eat them until he is purified, and only members of a priest's household may share them. Offerings brought by any Israelite or foreigner must be without defect to be accepted. Newborn animals must stay with their mothers for seven days, a mother and its young may not be slaughtered on the same day, and thank offerings must be eaten the day they are offered. The chapter closes with God's demand that his name be kept holy.
story: Chapter 21 set out who may serve as a priest. Chapter 22 continues the priestly section of the Holiness Code by turning to what the priests handle and eat: the portions of the offerings that the people bring to God, which became the priests' food. It then widens to the people themselves, since every worshiper chose the animal he brought. The chapter closes the unit that began in chapter 17 with a summary: God's name must not be profaned, because he is the LORD who sanctifies Israel and brought them out of Egypt. Chapter 23 will move from holy things to holy times.
historical:
Priests in Israel had no farmland of their own; the tribe of Levi received towns to live in but no tribal territory when the land was divided. They lived instead on portions of the offerings and on tithes (Numbers 18). That made the holy food their household's daily bread, and the rules about who could eat it were practical questions of family life. As with the chapters around it, traditional readers date these rules to Moses at Sinai, while many critical scholars date the Holiness Code in its final form to the late monarchy or the exile.

The temptation the chapter guards against was real. Around the fifth century BC, after the return from exile, the prophet Malachi accused the priests of his day of doing exactly what verses 20 to 25 forbid: "When you offer blind animals for sacrifice, is it not wrong? And when you present the lame and sick ones, is it not wrong?" (Malachi 1:8). He challenged them to try offering such animals to the Persian governor and see how he received them. The problem was not poverty but contempt: keeping the best animal and giving God what was left.
cultural:
Ritual uncleanness was a normal part of life, caused by skin disease, bodily discharges, contact with the dead, or touching certain creatures (Leviticus 11 to 15). It was not sin, but it made a person unfit for holy things until washing and the passing of time restored cleanness. A priest who was unclean simply had to wait until evening, bathe, and then eat (verses 6 and 7). The rules about who shared the priest's food follow the ancient household: a slave bought or born into the house was part of the family and ate with it, while a hired worker or a guest was not. A priest's daughter who married outside the priestly family ate at her husband's table, but if she was widowed or divorced without children and came home, she ate at her father's again.

The rules about animals show a concern that goes beyond ritual. An animal with a defect could not be offered to fulfill a vow, though one with a stunted limb could be given as a freewill offering (verse 23), an allowance for a gift given freely. Newborn animals stayed with their mothers seven days, and a mother and its young were not to be killed on the same day. Similar laws appear in Exodus 23:19 (not boiling a young goat in its mother's milk) and Deuteronomy 22:6-7 (letting the mother bird go). Jewish and Christian interpreters have seen in them a lesson in compassion toward animals, though others read them mainly as marking the boundary between life and death.
literary: The chapter has three speeches, each opened by "Then the LORD said to Moses" (verses 1, 17, and 26). The first (verses 1 to 16) is addressed to the priests and concerns eating holy food. The second (verses 17 to 25) is addressed to the priests and all Israel and concerns the condition of offerings. The third (verses 26 to 33) gives rules about newborn animals and thank offerings and then broadens into a closing exhortation. The refrain "I am the LORD" appears repeatedly, and the key terms profane, holy, and acceptable run through the whole. The ending (verses 31 to 33) gathers the entire section from chapter 17 onward into a single claim: God sanctifies Israel, he brought them out of Egypt, and his name must be acknowledged as holy among them.

outline.t: Priests must be clean to eat holy food
Who in the priest's household may eat
Newborn animals and the thank offering
Do not profane God's holy name

doctrines.note: Holy things are to be handled as holy. The chapter teaches that carelessness with what belongs to God is itself a way of profaning his name, and that God is the one who makes his people and priests holy.
An offering had to be without blemish to be accepted on the worshiper's behalf. Acceptance before God came through a whole, unblemished substitute, a principle the New Testament applies to Christ.

Verse 32 states God's purpose: "I must be acknowledged as holy among the Israelites." God's name, his revealed character and reputation, is at stake in how his people worship and live. Jewish tradition drew from this verse the ideas of sanctifying the Name and profaning it by one's conduct.

words.note: Tamim, unblemished, whole, complete. Used of sacrificial animals, it means without physical defect. Used of people, as of Noah (Genesis 6:9) and in God's command to Abraham (Genesis 17:1), it means blameless or wholehearted. The animal's wholeness pictured the wholeness God seeks in worshipers.

Ratson, acceptance or favor. An offering is brought so that it will be accepted on your behalf (verses 19, 20, 21, 29). The word shows that sacrifice was not a way to force God's hand; God decides what he accepts, and the worshiper's goodwill is shown by what he brings.

Qodesh, holiness or holy thing. In this chapter it often refers to the sacred offerings, the portions of sacrifices set aside for God and given to the priests. It occurs fourteen times, marking the whole chapter as concerned with what belongs to God.

Todah, thanksgiving or thank offering (verse 29), a kind of peace offering brought to give thanks for deliverance. It had to be eaten the same day, which in practice meant sharing it with family and friends. Several psalms speak of bringing such offerings after rescue.

christ: The New Testament applies the chapter's demand for an unblemished offering to Christ. Peter says believers were redeemed "with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Peter 1:19), and Hebrews speaks of Christ, "who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God" (Hebrews 9:14). The perfection required of every animal on the altar is found in him, not as a physical quality but as sinless obedience. The concern of verse 32, that God's name be acknowledged as holy, is the same concern that stands at the head of the Lord's Prayer, "hallowed be Your name" (Matthew 6:9). And the logic of Malachi's rebuke, not giving God the leftovers, is taken up in Paul's call to believers to offer their bodies "as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God" (Romans 12:1). Hebrews also calls praise "a sacrifice of praise" (Hebrews 13:15), echoing the thank offering of verse 29.
questions: Malachi accused Israel of offering God what they didn't want. Where are you tempted to give God your leftovers of time, money, or attention?
The chapter treats handling holy things carelessly as a way of profaning God's name. How can familiarity with sacred things lead to treating them as ordinary?
Verse 32 says God's name must be acknowledged as holy among his people. What in your life most affects whether others see God's character as holy or as ordinary?
